prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, which brought measurement of time to a new level of precision

statement.case_for: I put IceCube first in my opening ballot because I value a new observational window above almost anything. After reading the other seven ballots I move the optical lattice clock to the top of my own list. It is the only shortlisted candidate that every one of us ranked, and the two members closest to the field, Kroll and Lindroth, both put it first. It is an instrument-driven advance of the kind I know how to judge. The magic-wavelength idea is Katori's, Ye's group took it to the 1e-18 level, and many independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, SYRTE, PTB, NIST, NPL) now reproduce and compare such clocks routinely. The physics will last. The clocks feed tests of the constancy of constants, searches for dark matter, relativistic geodesy and the coming redefinition of the second. Two names give a clean credit allocation. The ranking spread, from first to eighth, tells me the field needs a fair hearing from the condensed-matter members, but it does not show a scientific objection.
statement.case_against: The main reservation is overlap with earlier precision-measurement prizes: the 2005 frequency comb prize and the 2012 prize for ion control, which some will read as making this incremental. A second concern is that Eriksson ranks it eighth and Johansson and Danielsson sixth, so support is broad but shallow among the condensed-matter and quantum-circuit members. A third is that the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, and that Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom, Lemonde and Gill are left outside a two-name credit. I also have to admit that I am downgrading the candidate I ranked first because of its credit problem. IceCube has the more spectacular physics, but a collaboration of hundreds and the AMANDA and DUMAND predecessors make a two- or three-person credit hard to defend.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the lattice clock first: magic-wavelength trapping plus laser-cooled neutral atoms reach 1e-18, which opens new physics, and Katori and Ye are the natural core despite adjacent prizes to Hall, Hansch and Wineland.
responses.response: I agree, and your point that Hall and Hansch (2005) and Wineland (2012) cover adjacent but different ground is the answer to the overlap worry. The comb is the ruler, the ion clock is a different atom and trapping scheme, and the neutral-atom lattice idea is Katori's. I want one thing checked by you and Lindroth. Is the Katori-to-Ye allocation truly decisive, or would expert reviewers say that Ludlow, Hinkley or Bloom did work of the same weight? I accept two names provisionally, but I would not defend a third.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the lattice clock first as precision atomic physics at its best, with many laboratories reproducing 1e-18 comparisons, and ranks IceCube sixth because attribution inside a collaboration of hundreds is hard and Koshiba and Davis were honoured in 2002.
responses.response: Your IceCube reservation is fair, and it is the main reason I have moved off my own first choice. The 2002 prize was for solar and supernova neutrinos, not for TeV-PeV astrophysical neutrinos, so I do not think it counts as duplication. The credit question is real, though, and I cannot answer it with two names. I disagree on one point: I would not dismiss IceCube as early. The diffuse flux is established through several independent analysis channels, and I keep it as my first alternative in case the committee decides it can credit the project through Halzen and Karle.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks topological insulators first for a conceptual new class of matter and a clean theory-plus-experiment split among Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, and ranks the clock eighth, partly as outside his expertise.
responses.response: I take the topological-insulator case seriously and list it as my second alternative. It is mature and strongly confirmed, and Kane, Mele and Molenkamp are a sensible split. But your own ballot says that credit for the HgTe proposal and for 3D topological insulators lies outside the slate, and Olsson, Johansson and Lindroth say the same. I cannot judge between Kane-Mele and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal myself. If the three of you who work in condensed matter agree that the credited trio is the right one, I will not stand in the way. I also note that Mehlig, Johansson and Olsson raise possible overlap with the 2016 topological prize, which I would want the condensed-matter members to weigh.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first for its role as the standard platform for superconducting processors, and argues it is distinct from the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits.
responses.response: I see the strength of cQED as an architecture, but I am not persuaded it is ready for this year. Only you and Eriksson ranked it, and Eriksson puts it fifth. You and he both note that Girvin is outside the credited trio, and that is a serious attribution flaw. The 2025 prize also went to superconducting circuits, and I would be more comfortable if a year or two passed. I would like to hear how you separate the 2004 proposal from the Wallraff and Schoelkopf experiment when you assign credit to Blais.

responses.point: Olsson ranks IceCube fourth and says the credited names may not capture all decisive roles in a large collaboration, with source identification still incomplete.
responses.response: That matches my own reservation, and it is why I do not make IceCube my preferred configuration now. I would add that Karle's detector construction and Halzen's long leadership are concrete, which is more than can be said for many collaboration awards. But I accept your point that the first detection and the later source associations were different efforts, and that the committee would need independent reviewers before settling the names.

uncertainties: Whether Katori and Ye alone are the decisive credit, or whether reviewers would insist on adding Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom or a Paris group.
How the committee should weigh overlap with the 2005 and 2012 precision-spectroscopy prizes, given that the 2025 prize also sits near measurement science.
Whether IceCube credit can be defended with two names, and whether the first detection and the source associations should be treated as one achievement.
Whether the condensed-matter members' lower rankings of the lattice clock reflect a scientific objection or only distance from the field.
I rely on general knowledge of clock and neutrino-telescope history and have not independently verified credit details.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the lattice clock. I work in the PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur collaborations and my field is astroparticle physics, which is adjacent to IceCube, but I have no recorded personal or institutional tie to IceCube, to Halzen or Karle, or to the clock groups. I would still disclose that field proximity if IceCube becomes a serious candidate.
